# Cross-language golden fixtures — the accounting atom

Go and Python cannot share code. They share **these files**.

`docs/PAPER_EXECUTION_CONTRACT.md` §5.1 states one formula, and two independent programs claim to
implement it: `services/prediction/app/backtest.py::net_returns` (the walk-forward gate and the
offline evaluator) and `paper/`'s live ledger. A live number and a backtest number can only
disagree *meaningfully* if the arithmetic underneath them is provably the same arithmetic.

```
prev[t]     = positions[t-1]                     (0 before the first bar)
turnover[t] = |positions[t] - prev[t]|
net[t]      = positions[t] * ret_next[t] - (cost_bps/10000) * turnover[t]
equity      = cumprod(1 + net)
a "trade"   = a transition INTO a nonzero position
```

## Who consumes them

| suite | file | what it asserts |
|---|---|---|
| Python | `services/prediction/tests/test_accounting_fixtures.py` | `backtest.net_returns` / `run_backtest` reproduce `expected` |
| Go | `paper/accounting_fixtures_test.go` | the **ledger**, driven bar by bar, reproduces `expected` from its own fills and marks |

The Go side is the interesting half: it does not call a Go copy of the formula and compare that.
It runs a real `Ledger` — real fills, real fees on real traded notional, real daily marks — and
then *re-derives* the per-bar net-return series from that bookkeeping (§5.5). If the ledger books a
fee at the wrong bar, misses a leg of a flip, or marks a position at the wrong price, the derived
series stops matching and the test fails. **If it cannot reproduce the atom from its own
bookkeeping, the ledger is wrong — not the fixture.**

## Where the numbers came from

They were **not** generated by either implementation. A fixture produced by the code under test
enshrines that code's bugs as truth. The expected values were computed from the formula above as
written in the contract, and `flat-long-flat.json` carries a `handComputation` block that works the
whole scenario out in arithmetic anybody can check by eye — so neither program is the authority.

The scenarios cover, at minimum: flat→long→flat, a flip, a short, costs charged on **both** legs of
a flip (zero returns, so every number in `net` is a cost), an all-flat series, and a multi-bar hold
at the shipped 6 bps that pins "no intra-hold rebalancing".

## Editing

Don't, casually. Changing an expected number changes what both implementations are held to. If a
fixture is wrong, fix it from the contract and say so in the commit — never from whichever program
happened to disagree.
